newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia rejects calls to delay July 19 poll.
newsitem.headline: Liberia rejects calls to delay July 19 poll.

text.p: Liberia on Monday rejected calls for a delay of elections on July 19 as a recipe for further trouble in the country emerging from seven years of civil war.
"The elections will take place unfailingly on July 19," declared elections commission chairman Harry Andrews, reacting to a campaign by 12 of 13 parties fielding candidates.
"I wish to assure the public that the holding of elections is firmly on course," Andrews told a news conference.
Liberia's dominant warlord Charles Taylor, a front-running presidential candidate, has given a clear warning of trouble if the presidential and parliamenetary elections were postponed.
"If Henry Andrews attempts to postpone these elections, only the angels, not even ECOMOG (peacekeepers) will protect him," Taylor said in a broadcast on state radio on Tuesday night.

"If he does I am going to provide him with money for his plane ticket to leave the country," added Taylor, who started civil war in December 1989 and is widely blamed for the breakdown of over a dozen previous peace deals.
Regional superpower Nigeria, which leads the ECOMOG West peacekeping force in Liberia, on Tuesday ruled out any delay in the elections wrapping up the latest peace accord.

The United States, which has historic ties with the West African country founded in 1847 by freed American slaves, has warned Liberians that Western nations funding the elections would not welcome a postponement of the vote.
Fighting has killed more than 150,000 people, shattered the economy and displaced a pre-war population of 2.5 million.
Supporters of a delay had denounced alleged fraud and irregularities during voter registration, which ended on Wednesday after a three-day extension.
But Andrews, a veteran Liberian journalist, described their campaign as "a calculated attempt to lead the Liberian public and create instability".

The 12 parties lobbying for a delay have been unable to hold planned meetings on Tuesday and Wednesday when they had hoped to suggest an alternative poll date. Political comentators said there appeared to be no agreement within the group on the length of the delay.
The Unity Party of Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman in the presidential race, said it had had convened a strategy meeting to react to the commission's statement.
Johnson-Sirleaf, a former United Nations official and ex-minister, is rated by many Liberians as Taylor's toughest rival in a field that includes two other prominent warlords.
